learn.hook: India started a national family planning programme in 1951, one of the first countries in the world to do so.
points: According to the World Health Organisation (WHO), reproductive health means total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A society with people having physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects is reproductively healthy.

India initiated action plans and programmes at a national level to attain total reproductive health in 1951 under the name 'family planning'. Improved programmes covering wider areas are now run as Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH) programmes.

Strategies: create awareness through audio-visual and print media with government and non-government agencies; parents, close relatives, teachers and friends also have a big role in sharing information.

Introduce sex education in schools to give correct information about reproductive organs, adolescence and related changes, safe and hygienic sexual practices, STDs and AIDS, so young people are not misled by myths and misconceptions.

Educate fertile couples and those of marriageable age about birth control options, care of pregnant mothers, post-natal care of mother and child, importance of breastfeeding and equal opportunities for male and female children; spread awareness about problems of uncontrolled population growth and social evils like sex abuse and sex-related crimes.

example.q: A school plans a reproductive-health week. Suggest three activities that match the strategies in NCERT.
steps: Awareness: poster and video sessions with help from health agencies.
Sex education: a doctor explains adolescence, reproductive organs, safe and hygienic practices and STIs, busting myths.
Social messages: talks on equal opportunity for girls and boys and on the problems of uncontrolled population growth.
example.answer: Awareness sessions, factual sex education by experts, and talks on gender equality and population issues.

learn.reallife: School health programmes such as Ayushman Bharat's School Health and Wellness initiative give adolescents accurate, age-appropriate information, replacing playground myths.

topics.title: Amniocentesis ban and gains in reproductive health

learn.hook: A test meant to detect genetic disorders was misused to identify the sex of a foetus, so India banned that particular use by law.
points: Amniocentesis is a foetal test based on the chromosomal pattern in the amniotic fluid surrounding the developing embryo. It can detect genetic disorders.
There is a statutory (legal) ban on amniocentesis for sex determination, to check the rise in female foeticide. Massive child immunisation is another major step.

Research on reproduction-related areas is encouraged by government and non-government agencies to find newer methods. For example, Saheli, a new oral contraceptive for females, was developed by scientists at the Central Drug Research Institute (CDRI), Lucknow.

Results: better awareness about sex-related matters; more medically assisted deliveries and better post-natal care, lowering maternal and infant mortality rates; more couples with small families; better detection and cure of STDs; increased medical facilities for sex-related problems.

example.q: Why is amniocentesis allowed for detecting genetic disorders but banned for sex determination?
steps: Detecting chromosomal or genetic disorders helps doctors and parents manage health risks.
Using it to find the foetus's sex was leading to selective abortion of female foetuses.
The statutory ban targets the misuse, protecting the sex ratio and the rights of girls.
example.answer: Medical use protects health; the ban stops misuse for sex determination and female foeticide.

learn.reallife: Signboards in Indian clinics read 'Sex determination is a punishable offence' because of this ban.

learn.hook: According to NCERT, India's population was about 350 million at Independence and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011.
points: Better living conditions led to a population explosion. Causes: a rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR), and an increase in the number of people in the reproductive age.

NCERT figures: world population about 2 billion in 1900, about 6 billion by 2000 and 7.2 billion in 2011. India: about 350 million at Independence, close to the billion mark by 2000, and over 1.2 billion by May 2011.
The 2011 census shows India's population growth rate was less than 2 per cent, i.e. 20/1000/year. Uncontrolled growth leads to scarcity of basic requirements like food, shelter and clothing.

Measures: motivating smaller families with contraceptive methods; slogans like 'Hum Do Hamare Do' and many urban couples adopting a 'one child norm'; statutory raising of the marriageable age of females to 18 years and of males to 21 years; incentives given to couples with small families.

example.q: A growth rate of 20 per 1000 per year is the same as what percentage? If a town has 50,000 people, how many are added in a year at this rate?
example.answer: 2 per cent; about 1000 people per year.

learn.reallife: The National Family Health Survey (NFHS) tracks India's falling fertility rate; many states have now reached replacement-level fertility.

topics.title: The ideal contraceptive and natural methods

learn.hook: Not every method of family planning needs a pharmacy; some depend only on understanding the body's own cycle.
points: An ideal contraceptive should be user-friendly, easily available, effective and reversible, with no or least side effects, and it should in no way interfere with sexual drive, desire or the sexual act of the user.
Contraceptive methods are classified as natural/traditional, barrier, IUDs, oral contraceptives, injectables, implants and surgical methods.

Natural methods avoid meeting of ovum and sperms. Periodic abstinence: avoiding coitus from day 10 to 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected (the fertile period). Withdrawal or coitus interruptus: the male withdraws his penis before ejaculation.

Lactational amenorrhea: absence of menstruation during intense lactation following parturition. Since ovulation and the cycle do not occur, chances of conception are almost nil. It is theoretically effective only up to a maximum of six months after parturition, as long as the mother breastfeeds the child fully.
Natural methods have almost no side effects, but their chances of failure are high.

example.q: A woman has a regular 28-day cycle. Using periodic abstinence as described in NCERT, which days should be avoided and why?
steps: Ovulation is expected around day 14.
NCERT advises avoiding coitus from day 10 to day 17, the fertile period around ovulation.
example.answer: Days 10 to 17, because chances of fertilisation are very high around ovulation.

learn.reallife: ASHA workers counsel new mothers that lactational amenorrhea protects only for a limited time, so a planned method is needed after that.

learn.hook: A small copper-bearing device placed in the uterus is among the most widely accepted contraceptive methods in India.
points: Barrier methods physically prevent ovum and sperms from meeting. Condoms are barriers of thin rubber or latex used to cover the penis in males or the vagina and cervix in females just before coitus, so semen is not released into the female tract. 'Nirodh' is a popular brand for males.
Condoms also safeguard the user from contracting STIs and AIDS. Both male and female condoms are disposable and can be self-inserted, giving privacy to the user.

Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults are rubber barriers inserted into the female reproductive tract to cover the cervix during coitus, blocking sperm entry. They are reusable. Spermicidal creams, jellies and foams are usually used with them to increase efficiency.

Intrauterine devices (IUDs) are inserted by doctors or expert nurses into the uterus through the vagina. Types: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20).

IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus. Released Cu ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. Hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms. IUDs suit females who want to delay pregnancy and/or space children.

steps: Non-medicated: Lippes loop.

example.answer: Non-medicated: Lippes loop; Copper: Multiload 375, Cu7; Hormonal: Progestasert, LNG-20

topics.title: Pills, injectables, emergency and surgical methods

learn.hook: A once-a-week contraceptive pill developed in Lucknow is called Saheli, meaning 'friend'.
points: Oral contraceptives contain progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations. They are taken daily for 21 days, starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle; after a gap of 7 days (during which menstruation occurs) the course is repeated. They inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent or retard entry of sperms.

Saheli, the new oral contraceptive for females, contains a non-steroidal preparation and is a 'once a week' pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. It was developed at CDRI, Lucknow.

Progestogens alone or with oestrogen can also be used as injections or implants under the skin, acting like pills over a longer period. Progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations or IUDs used within 72 hours of coitus are very effective emergency contraceptives, used after rape or casual unprotected intercourse.

Surgical (terminal) methods, or sterilisation, are for those who want no more children. Vasectomy: a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum. Tubectomy: a small part of the fallopian tube is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina. They are highly effective, but reversibility is very poor.

Possible side effects of contraceptives include nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding and even breast cancer. So contraceptives should be used only after proper medical advice.

example.q: Name the method: (a) part of the vas deferens tied through a scrotal incision; (b) pill taken weekly; (c) used within 72 hours after unprotected coitus.
steps: (a) Cutting or tying the vas deferens is vasectomy.
(b) The non-steroidal weekly pill is Saheli.
(c) Hormones or an IUD used within 72 hours act as emergency contraceptives.

learn.reallife: India's family planning programme offers both vasectomy and tubectomy free at government hospitals; no-scalpel vasectomy is promoted because it is quick and minimally invasive.

learn.hook: Laws on MTP aim at one goal: reducing unsafe abortions that endanger women's lives.
points: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion. Nearly 45 to 50 million MTPs are performed in a year worldwide, about one-fifth of all conceived pregnancies.

India legalised MTP in 1971 with strict conditions. NCERT describes the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017: a pregnancy may be terminated within the first 12 weeks on the opinion of one registered medical practitioner; between 12 and 24 weeks, two registered medical practitioners must agree that the grounds exist. (The law was updated again in 2021; for board answers, use the NCERT version.)

Grounds: continuing the pregnancy would risk the woman's life or cause grave injury to her physical or mental health; or there is substantial risk that the child would suffer from serious physical or mental abnormalities.

MTP helps get rid of unwanted pregnancies due to casual unprotected intercourse or failure of contraception, and in cases where continuation could be harmful or fatal to the mother, the foetus or both. MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester (up to 12 weeks).

Concerns: misuse to abort normal female foetuses; many MTPs performed illegally by unqualified quacks, which are unsafe and could be fatal; emotional, ethical, religious and social issues. Using MTP as a contraceptive substitute is dangerous; counselling and safe facilities are important.

example.q: According to NCERT's description of the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2017, how many registered medical practitioners must give an opinion for terminating a pregnancy of (a) 10 weeks and (b) 18 weeks?
steps: (a) 10 weeks is within the first 12 weeks: one registered medical practitioner.
(b) 18 weeks lies between 12 and 24 weeks: two registered medical practitioners.

learn.reallife: The law aims to move abortions from unsafe quacks to qualified doctors in registered facilities, protecting women's lives.

learn.hook: NCERT notes that STIs are most common in the 15 to 24 age group, which is why correct information matters early.
points: Infections transmitted through sexual intercourse are called sexually transmitted infections (STIs), venereal diseases (VD) or reproductive tract infections (RTI). Examples: gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV leading to AIDS.
Some, like hepatitis-B and HIV, also spread by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments with infected persons, transfusion of blood, or from an infected mother to the foetus.
Except for hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV infections, the other diseases are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.

Early symptoms are often minor: itching, fluid discharge, slight pain and swellings in the genital region. Infected females may be asymptomatic, so the disease stays undetected. Social stigma also stops people from seeking timely treatment. Untreated STIs can lead to pelvic inflammatory diseases (PID), abortions, still births, ectopic pregnancies, infertility or even cancer of the reproductive tract.
Prevention: avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always try to use condoms during coitus; in case of doubt, go to a qualified doctor for early detection and complete treatment.

example.q: Which of these STIs are NOT completely curable even when detected early: gonorrhoea, genital herpes, syphilis, hepatitis-B, HIV, chlamydiasis?
steps: NCERT exceptions: hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV.
Gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydiasis are completely curable if detected early.

learn.reallife: NACO and state health departments run free, confidential STI clinics (Suraksha clinics) so young people can get tested without fear of stigma.

learn.hook: The world's first IVF baby was born in 1978; today Indian IVF clinics help thousands of couples every year.
points: Infertility: many couples cannot produce children in spite of unprotected sexual co-habitation. Causes may be physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or even psychological. In India the female is often blamed, but the cause can lie with either partner; NCERT stresses that very often the problem lies with the male partner.
Specialised health care units (infertility clinics) can diagnose and correct some disorders; where no correction is possible, assisted reproductive technologies (ART) can help.

In vitro fertilisation (IVF) is fertilisation outside the body in conditions similar to those in the body, followed by embryo transfer (ET). It is popularly called the 'test tube baby' programme. Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and induced to form a zygote in the laboratory.

ZIFT (zygote intra fallopian transfer): the zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube. IUT (intra uterine transfer): embryos with more than 8 blastomeres are transferred into the uterus.

example.q: An IVF lab has two embryos: one at 6 blastomeres and one at 32 blastomeres. Which transfer technique suits each?
steps: Up to 8 blastomeres → ZIFT, into the fallopian tube.
More than 8 blastomeres → IUT, into the uterus.

learn.reallife: Indian regulation of ART clinics, under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021, sets standards so couples receive safe, ethical treatment.

topics.title: GIFT, ICSI, artificial insemination and limits of ART

learn.hook: Science can now inject a single sperm into an ovum with a needle thinner than a hair. That is ICSI.
points: Embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation (fusion of gametes within the female) can also be used for such transfers to help females who cannot conceive.

GIFT (gamete intra fallopian transfer): an ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of another female who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and further development.
ICSI (intra cytoplasmic sperm injection): a specialised procedure in which a sperm is directly injected into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory.

Artificial insemination (AI): used when the male partner cannot inseminate the female or has a very low sperm count. Semen from the husband or a healthy donor is artificially introduced into the vagina or into the uterus; the latter is IUI (intra-uterine insemination).

Limitations of ART: needs extremely high precision handling by specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so facilities exist only in few centres and are affordable to limited people; emotional, religious and social factors also deter. Legal adoption is one of the best options for couples seeking parenthood, as many orphaned and destitute children need care.

example.q: Match each problem to an ART: (a) very low sperm count; (b) a woman cannot produce ova but her tubes and uterus are healthy; (c) sperms cannot penetrate the ovum on their own.
steps: (a) Low sperm count: artificial insemination, e.g. IUI.
(b) No ova but suitable environment: GIFT with a donor ovum.
(c) Sperms unable to fertilise: ICSI, injecting a sperm into the ovum.

learn.reallife: India's Juvenile Justice Act and the CARA portal let couples legally adopt children, which NCERT highlights as a valuable alternative to ART.

games.title: What is transferred?
items: GIFT
AI
IUI
ZIFT
IUT

quiz.q: In ICSI,
options: an ovum is placed in the fallopian tube
semen is placed in the uterus
a sperm is directly injected into the ovum
an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is placed in the uterus
quiz.explain: ICSI = intra cytoplasmic sperm injection: one sperm is injected into the ovum's cytoplasm.
steps: ICSI = intra cytoplasmic sperm injection
A single sperm is injected directly into the ovum in the lab
Answer: a sperm is directly injected into the ovum
quiz.mistake: Confuses ICSI with IUI or IUT

quiz.q: GIFT involves
options: transfer of a zygote into the uterus
transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube of another female
injection of a sperm into the ovum
introduction of semen into the vagina
quiz.explain: In GIFT a gamete (ovum) is transferred so that fertilisation can occur in the recipient's tube.
steps: GIFT = gamete intra fallopian transfer
A donor ovum is placed in the fallopian tube of a female who cannot make ova
Answer: transfer of an ovum collected from a donor into the fallopian tube of another female
quiz.mistake: Thinks GIFT transfers an embryo

quiz.q: Artificial insemination is advised when
options: the embryo has more than 8 blastomeres
the male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count
quiz.explain: AI introduces semen from the husband or a donor into the vagina or uterus.
steps: AI is for when the male cannot inseminate the female
Or when he has a very low sperm count
Answer: the male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count
quiz.mistake: Applies AI to female-factor problems

quiz.q: Semen artificially introduced into the uterus is called
quiz.explain: IUI is intra-uterine insemination, a form of artificial insemination.
steps: Artificial insemination puts semen into the vagina or the uterus
Into the uterus = intra-uterine insemination
Answer: IUI
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the ART abbreviations

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of ART mentioned by NCERT?
options: It is available free in every village
It needs specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so it is available in few centres
It works for every couple instantly
quiz.explain: High precision, cost and limited centres restrict access; emotional, religious and social factors also deter.
steps: ART needs highly precise handling by specialists and costly instruments
So it exists in few centres and few can afford it
Answer: It needs specialised professionals and expensive instruments, so it is available in few centres
quiz.mistake: Overestimates ART access

quiz.q: NCERT suggests which alternative for couples looking for parenthood?
quiz.explain: Legal adoption gives care to orphaned and destitute children and parenthood to couples.
steps: NCERT: many orphaned and destitute children need care
Legal adoption is one of the best options for parenthood
Answer: Legal adoption
quiz.mistake: Does not recall adoption as an option

quiz.q: Which of these ARTs involves fertilisation occurring inside the female body?
quiz.explain: In GIFT, the donor ovum is placed in the fallopian tube where fertilisation can occur; the others involve lab fertilisation.
steps: IVF, ICSI and ZIFT all form the zygote in the laboratory
In GIFT the donor ovum is put in the tube, so fertilisation happens inside the body
Answer: GIFT
quiz.mistake: Does not distinguish in vivo from in vitro fertilisation

quiz.q: Which ART uses embryos formed by in vivo fertilisation?
options: Embryo transfer to a female who cannot conceive
quiz.explain: Embryos formed in vivo (within a female) can be transferred to help females who cannot conceive.
steps: In vivo = fusion of gametes inside a female
Such embryos can also be transferred to females who cannot conceive
ICSI and AI are not embryo transfers
Answer: Embryo transfer to a female who cannot conceive
quiz.mistake: Confuses embryo transfer with sperm-based methods

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Explain GIFT, ICSI and IUI. Is ART for everyone, or are there limits?'
teach.praise: Excellent! GIFT moves an ovum, ICSI injects a sperm, IUI places semen in the uterus, and cost limits access, so adoption is a great option.
teach.nudge: Good! Which technique injects a sperm into an ovum, and what does NCERT suggest besides ART?

revise.summary: GIFT places a donor ovum in a recipient's fallopian tube, ICSI injects a sperm into the ovum, and artificial insemination (including IUI) introduces semen into the vagina or uterus. ART is costly and limited, so legal adoption is a good option.
remember: GIFT = donor ovum → fallopian tube
ICSI = sperm injected into ovum
IUI = semen into the uterus (for low sperm count)
traps: GIFT transfers a gamete, not a zygote
ICSI is not insemination; fertilisation happens in the lab
